# VDPP, LLC v. VOLKSWAGEN GROUP OF AMERICA, INC. , 24-2226 (Fed. Cir. 2026)
**Court:** U.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit

**Docket Number:** 24-2226

**Date Decided:** August 19, 2026

Justia Opinion Summary
A company holding a patent for electrically controlled spectacles filed a lawsuit against a car manufacturer, alleging patent infringement. The plaintiff, represented by its counsel, sought damages for alleged infringement and included a request for pre-suit damages. The defendant moved to dismiss the complaint for failure to state a claim and for improper venue. In response, the plaintiff requested leave to amend its complaint and filed a proposed amended complaint.
The plaintiff had previously entered into several settlement agreements licensing the patent to third parties. At the United States District Court for the Southern District of Texas, the judge dismissed the case with prejudice under Rule 12(b)(6), finding that the plaintiff’s proposed amended complaint was futile because it failed to adequately plead compliance with the patent marking requirements under 35 U.S.C. § 287(a), particularly regarding its licensees.
The court denied leave to amend, denied a motion to amend the judgment, awarded attorney fees to the defendant under 35 U.S.C. § 285, and sanctioned plaintiff’s counsel, holding both the plaintiff and counsel jointly and severally liable for the attorney fees.
On appeal, the United States Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit affirmed the district court’s dismissal of the complaint without leave to amend, agreeing that amendment would have been futile due to the failure to plead compliance with § 287(a). The appellate court also affirmed the award of attorney fees, finding no abuse of discretion in the determination that the case was exceptional due to the plaintiff’s unreasonable litigation conduct.

# VDPP, LLC v. Volkswagen Group of America, Inc.
August 19, 2026 ·24-2226 ·Panel Decision · By Maria Santos

The United States Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit affirmed the dismissal of a patent infringement complaint and an award of attorney fees. The court dismissed the portion of the appeal regarding sanctions against the plaintiff's counsel for lack of jurisdiction.
## Background
In two thousand and twenty-three, VDPP sued Volkswagen for alleged infringement of a patent relating to electrically controlled spectacles. The district court dismissed the complaint without leave to amend, awarded Volkswagen attorney fees under Section two hundred eighty-five of Title thirty-five, and sanctioned VDPP’s counsel under Section one thousand nine hundred twenty-seven of Title twenty-eight and the court’s inherent power.
## The court’s reasoning
The Federal Circuit reviewed the dismissal de novo under Fifth Circuit law, finding the proposed amendment futile because VDPP failed to allege that its licensees complied with the notice provision of Section two hundred eighty-seven of Title thirty-five. The court affirmed the attorney fee award, agreeing the case was exceptional due to frivolous positions and a pattern of litigation abuse.

  Six petitions for rehearing or rehearing en banc are currently pending before the Federal Circuit in patent cases.  I wanted to do a quick run through to highlight the unusual concentration of vehicles for doctrinal correction.

 En Banc Rehearing at the Federal Circuit: Federal Rule of Appellate Procedure 35 and Federal Circuit Rule 35 govern  en banc rehearing. A petition must demonstrate that the panel decision conflicts with a prior decision of the court or that the case presents a question of exceptional importance. The full court, including senior judges who participated in the panel, votes on whether to grant. A grant requires a majority of judges in regular active service. jina.title: VDPP v. Volkswagen: Patent Owners Must Plead Licensees’ Compliance with Marking Requirements to Seek Pre-Suit Damages | Fenwick
jina.snippet:
[](https://www.fenwick.com/insights/publications/vdpp-v-volkswagen-patent-owners-must-plead-licensees-compliance-marking#main-content)

*   The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit held that a patent owner seeking past damages for infringement must plead compliance with the notice provision of 35 U.S.C. §287(a). That includes facts showing that any licensees to the patent also complied, not just the patent owner itself.
*   The decision leaves open whether patent owners can satisfy §287 through “reasonable efforts” short of requiring marking in every license agreement, a question that may be answered in future cases.

In [_VDPP, LLC v. Volkswagen Group of America, Inc._](https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/appellate-courts/cafc/24-2226/24-2226-2026-08-19.html), the Federal Circuit held that the district court did not abuse its discretion in dismissing VDPP’s complaint without leave to amend because VDPP did not, and could not, plead compliance with the notice provision of §287(a) that included compliance by VDPP’s licensees.

## The Marking Requirement

Under §287, a patentee cannot recover damages for infringement that occurred before it placed the defendant on notice of its infringement. Such notice may be provided by marking patented articles with the patent number or by filing an action for infringement. In [_Arctic Cat Inc. v. Bombardier Recreational Products Inc._](https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/appellate-courts/cafc/19-1080/19-1080-2020-02-19.html), 950 F.3d 860, 863–64 (Fed. Cir. 2020), the Federal Circuit held that a patentee who never makes or sells a patented article may recover pre-suit damages even without giving notice, but any licensees must also comply with the statute and mark their articles, and their failure to do so bars pre-suit damages for the patentee.

Under _Arctic Cat_, the court held that even though the burden of compliance falls on the patentee, the defendant must first “articulate the products it believes are unmarked.”

jina.title: Patent marking and licensing lessons from VDPP v Volkswagen
jina.snippet:
Imagine this scenario: you settled a patent dispute. You signed the agreement, banked the cheque and moved on.

In the eyes of the law, you just became a licensor – and that status carries an obligation of which most founders have never heard.

On 19 August 2026, the Federal Circuit decided _VDPP v Volkswagen Group of America_ (24-2226, Moore, Lourie; Cunningham, JJ). The court affirmed dismissal of VDPP’s infringement suit over US patent 9,426,452, a patent on electrically controlled spectacles and affirmed a US$207,543.60 attorney-fee award against VDPP.

The patent was not invalidated. Prior art played no role. VDPP lost on something that looks administrative:patent marking under 35 USC section 287(a).

## A settlement licence is still a licence

VDPP had signed 11 settlement agreements licensing its patent. While to VDPP, these may have seemed like closed chapters, the Federal Circuit saw 11 active licensing relationships, each carrying marking compliance obligations.

VDPP argued that these licences were different because they came out of settlements and no licensee admitted infringement. The court rejected both arguments. A settlement licence is no different for marking purposes from any other patent licence. The court’s own precedent frames a licence as a promise not to sue. The label on the document does not matter.

The ‘452 patent had expired, so the only remedy available was back damages for pre-suit infringement. Because no licensee marked and VDPP failed to plead compliance, those pre-suit damages vanished. With nothing else on the table, the case collapsed.

If your patent is near expiration, pre-suit damages are the only damages you have. Marking failures eliminate them entirely.

_Authored by Thomas Cunningham and Brady Cunningham_

The Federal Circuit’s recent decision in _VDPP, LLC v. Volkswagen Grp. of Am., Inc_. expands 35 U.S.C. §287’ marking requirement beyond patentees’ own products and traditional licenses. 186 F.4th 1372, 1377–80 (Fed. Cir. 2026). A settlement, covenant, or similar authorization to practice a patent may trigger marking obligations, even for non-practicing entities. Patent owners therefore must address marking in settlement agreements, impose obligations on authorized parties, and document reasonable compliance efforts. For accused infringers, _VDPP_ makes marking a potential threshold defense, not merely a damages issue. Inadequate allegations concerning licensee marking may foreclose pre-suit damages at the pleading stage and, in appropriate cases, support an exceptional-case finding.

**Patent Marking Is Not a Technicality. It Is a Damages Strategy.**

For many patent owners, patent marking is treated as an administrative afterthought. Products are marked, virtual-marking webpages are created, and the issue often disappears into the broader category of portfolio maintenance. Yet few provisions of the Patent Act can have a greater impact on the amount of money a patent owner ultimately recovers in litigation.

Under 35 U.S.C. § 287, a patent owner’s failure to comply with patent-marking requirements may eliminate years of recoverable damages. In *VDPP, LLC v. Volkswagen Group of America, Inc*., 186 F.4th 1372 (Fed. In so doing, the court rejected arguments that § 287’s marking provision was not triggered because the licenses were executed to settle litigation or because the licenses did not admit infringement.

In *VDPP*, the district court held that VDPP failed to state a claim, because VDPP did not comply with the marking statute before the asserted patent expired, and the proposed amended complaint was futile. Under the facts of this case, we see no way for VDPP to amend its complaint to plausibly allege it made reasonable efforts to ensure its licensees complied with 35 U.S.C. § 287.
